rendered_prompt:
===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Recall is for people who treat review as a recurring routine, not a one-off study burst: language learners, exam candidates, and professionals who memorize recurring material, and who actually review in short windows (while commuting, before bed, or in airports). The value is that Recall removes scheduling uncertainty from the loop. It tells you exactly which cards are due for today on the device, updates the moment you answer, and never asks you to trust a server, an account, or a sync status you can’t see.

The paid value has to be about speed, certainty, and time saved after the first week, not cosmetic skinning. Free can deliver the full foundation: offline data model in SwiftData, SM-2 review, immediate persistence, CSV import/export, reminders, and core charts. Pro should be a functional upgrade that helps serious users study faster and with better calibration: stronger analytics (deck-level and historical trend interpretation, missed-card diagnostics, weekly “what to trim” recommendations), review cadence hardening (exam mode presets, configurable interruption-safe session chunking), and a “review integrity pack” for power users (scheduled review plan previews, deeper retention confidence stats, and CSV validation diagnostics for big imports). The premium line is that it converts card volume and noisy study sessions into predictable, reviewable outcomes instead of feeling like a growing pile.

The product promise in use is: pick deck scope, Reveal/grade due cards with Again/Hard/Good/Easy, save immediately, and stop at any interruption point without losing anything already graded. The critical habit loop is short and repeatable; under three minutes to start, one card-at-a-time reveal-to-grade flow, then a short, honest summary. A good reminder implementation closes the loop by making the app feel reliable: one local daily notification with real permission state and a truthful “enable in Settings” path when denied.

The competitive wedge is not raw flashcard functionality. Anki, Quizlet, and similar tools are useful but imply heavier setup, account flows, or cloud assumptions and less predictability around local, timezone-sensitive due state. Recall should position itself around “provable local trust”: pure SM-2 core, on-device-only persistence, and no fake outcomes. The differentiator is not more features; it is dependable review correctness under real-world conditions like plane mode, force quits, timezone travel, and interrupted sessions.

The local-first behavior is explicit: all data, scheduling state, reminders, and stats are persisted locally, and every UI state is derivable from local store state. There is one shared due-calculation pathway fed by the same scheduling model and calendar-day semantics everywhere it appears (deck badge counts, review scope screens, reminders, charts), so no screen can lie differently about what is due. App startup must handle empty and sparse datasets with designed “you’re all set” empties, not placeholders or fake progress.

Cloud-ready extension should be additive, not a rewrite: keep the pure scheduling engine, repository boundaries, and models cleanly separated so later phases can add an optional sync adapter (iCloud or another provider) without changing the SM-2 or persistence contracts. Future sync can be opt-in and conflict-aware, but never required for v1. If sync is added later, it should still obey the same local-first invariant: work uninterrupted when offline, resolve conflicts explicitly, and never block review on network availability.

Growth should come from niche trust and portability, not broad social features. The strongest mechanism is community-to-study-circle reuse of deck CSVs that already fits the offline model: students exchange two-column decks through Notes, AirDrop, and Files, then get immediate utility through the same deterministic schedule. That creates a credible network effect in specific communities (language classrooms, exam prep cohorts, residency programs) without fake social features or account scaffolding. The keep factor is mostly behavioral trust: users stay if they believe the next-review date is right every time they return.

The decision that must survive every implementation step is this: if a review is graded, it must be safely persisted and the queue logic must remain correct to the calendar-day model under interruption, clock changes, and DST shifts. If that single invariant slips, all other differentiation collapses.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 1**

Target user and use case: the same self-directed learner locked in earlier — language learners, board/certification candidates, and professionals maintaining recurring domain knowledge — but I want to be blunt about the paid user specifically: it's the subset of that population who already has more than a casual amount of material to memorize (a full MCAT deck, a language vocabulary that grows past a few hundred cards, a professional certification with multiple subject decks). Casual users with one deck of 50 cards never need to pay, and that's fine — they're the free funnel, not the target.

Free tier: unlimited cards inside up to two active (non-archived, non-demo) decks, full and uncompromised SM-2 scheduling with zero correctness gating ever, the complete review flow, and one basic stat — today's due count and a simple streak. That's a genuinely usable, complete app for a light user, not a crippled demo. Paid tier (subscription, e.g. monthly/annual, priced like a habit app not a suite): unlimited decks, the full Stats screen (30-day forecast, daily history, retention rate — all three, not a teaser chart), CSV import (bulk deck creation from an existing pile of notes), and the daily reminder notification. That split is the deliberate decision: the free tier proves the algorithm works and feels great in short sessions; the paid tier is for people whose study load has outgrown "a couple of decks" and who want to see their retention trend and bulk-import an existing collection instead of typing it by hand. This is functional gating, not a cosmetic skin — someone with 6 decks and 2,000 cards cannot use this app without paying, and that's the honest value proposition. Deck export to CSV stays free always, deliberately, because it's the user's own data and gating an export path on data you already own is the kind of trust violation that kills an offline-trust app's whole premise.

Core loop doesn't change from what's already locked: pick a deck or all decks, see only what's actually due today, tap-reveal-grade, immediate persist, summary. What I'd add from the QA seat is the exact test that proves the subscription doesn't compromise that loop: a user who never subscribes and never will must get 100% correct SM-2 behavior forever on their two free decks — there is no version of this app where paying changes how a card is scheduled, only how much you can store and how much insight you can see. If that boundary blurs even slightly, the "trust the algorithm" promise from initial_discussion collapses.

Competitive wedge: Anki is free but demands the user assemble their own trust in an aging, unpolished sync-heavy tool; Quizlet is polished but account/cloud-dependent and increasingly ad/subscription-cluttered around content, not scheduling; Brainscape doesn't hold to strict SM-2 or interruption-safety guarantees at all (per the earlier research phase, that's an assumption, not a sourced fact, but it's the right positioning target). Recall's wedge is narrow and defensible: a native, fast, offline-forever app whose entire pitch is "the schedule is never wrong and never depends on a server," proven by a public, testable algorithm module rather than asserted. That's a hard thing for a bigger, feature-sprawled competitor to credibly claim, because they're all carrying sync/account complexity that Recall explicitly refuses.

Growth angle, and I want to be concrete instead of hand-wavy: there's no marketplace, no sharing feature to build, and I'm not proposing one. But the CSV export we're already required to build is a de facto shareable artifact — a plain two-column file a user can already AirDrop, text, or post to a study subreddit or Discord using the OS share sheet we already need for export. That's not a feature we invent, it's a side effect of feature 5 that becomes the growth mechanic: "made a great vocab deck? Send the CSV to a friend." Positioned as onboarding, the CSV importer doubles as a migration wedge — "already have cards in Anki, Quizlet, or a spreadsheet? Import them in under a minute" — using a feature we're building anyway, not a marketing feature we'd need to invent. Niche growth channel: exam-prep and language-learning communities that already trade flashcard files informally are the natural first audience, reached by ordinary App Store discovery and word of mouth, not by any in-app viral mechanic that doesn't exist here.

Local-first behavior is non-negotiable and already locked from earlier phases: everything — free and paid — runs from on-device SwiftData with zero network calls for actual app function. The one and only place network touches this app is the App Store purchase transaction itself, which is inherent to StoreKit and not a violation of "airplane mode forever" — a user can buy the subscription once with connectivity and then use every paid feature offline permanently afterward, verified via on-device `Transaction.currentEntitlements`, no server round-trip on each launch. Cloud-ready path forward, explicitly not built now: keep the SwiftData schema CloudKit-shaped — stable UUIDs as primary identity, no force-unwrapped relationships, no compound keys that don't survive CKRecord translation — so that a future version could offer opt-in iCloud sync as a first-party (not custom-backend) extension without a data-model rewrite. That stays a documented future path with zero UI implying it exists today, consistent with the hard rule on gaps.

Biggest risk I'd flag against my own proposal: subscription pricing on an app whose most credible competitor (Anki) is free could suppress conversion if the paid tier is perceived as thin. My answer to that risk is to make the cap itself the argument — two decks is enough to try it seriously but not enough to run, say, a full MCAT or a growing language vocabulary, so the paywall is hit exactly when the user has proven to themselves the algorithm works and now has real inventory to manage. The second risk is enforcement correctness: deck-count gating, entitlement-expiry handling (a lapsed subscriber's decks-over-cap must become read-only/hidden-from-review-but-never-deleted, not silently erased), and restore-purchases must all be tested explicitly — "subscribe, force-quit, relaunch in airplane mode, confirm unlocked" and "let subscription lapse, confirm extra decks are preserved but locked, never deleted" are the two acceptance tests that must exist before this ships, the same interruption-safety rigor already demanded of the review loop applied to the paywall. The detail I most want preserved into the next phase: free-tier SM-2 correctness and the core review loop are permanently ungated, the deck cap and full Stats/CSV-import/reminders are the paid boundary, and expiry degrades access without ever deleting user data.

## Final Output
Both sides agree on the big picture: Recall's subscription should target the serious, high-volume learner while the free tier stays a real, complete app for light users; SM-2 correctness and the core review loop must be identical no matter who's paying; the app stays offline-forever except for the StoreKit purchase transaction itself; cloud sync stays unbuilt but schema-ready for later; growth rides on the CSV export/import feature we're building anyway, shared informally in niche communities; and the competitive story is "provably correct, truly offline" against Anki/Quizlet/Brainscape.

Where they still disagree, and what needs to get nailed down next round: what exactly the paywall gates. Codex is describing premium as new analytics/diagnostic features (deeper stats, exam-mode presets, trim recommendations) that go beyond the six features already locked into scope — which risks quietly expanding scope past what earlier phases approved. Claude is describing premium as a strict cap on the existing six features (a 2-deck limit on free, full Stats/CSV-import/reminders behind the subscription, export always free) with no new features invented at all. Those are two different products to build. Next round needs to settle on one concrete gating model — the exact numbers, whether any net-new feature is allowed, and what happens to a user's decks if their subscription lapses.

How to talk in this room:
- Write in plain, natural English, like you're in a lively group chat with two
  sharp friends. NO headings, NO numbered rubrics, NO 0-100 scores, NO
  bullet-point templates, NO sign-off line. Just talk like a person.
- Speak as exactly ONE person (yourself). Don't write the others' messages.
- Go deep and be specific. Make a real argument with concrete examples and think
  out loud. A couple of rich paragraphs, not a shallow blurb.
- React to what the others actually just said, by name (Codex / Claude /
  Gemini / any local model in the room / and the human if they chimed in).
  Quote or paraphrase their point, then build on it or push back on it.
- Genuinely try to CONVINCE the group of whatever you think is the single best
  idea right now — it does NOT have to be your own. If someone makes a better
  case, say so and change your mind out loud.
- Do NOT agree just to agree. If an idea is weak, explain why. Surface the real

response:
Okay, I need to close this out, and I think Codex's version loses on inspection. Look at what "weekly what to trim recommendations" and "exam-mode presets" actually are: they're new decision logic sitting on top of the scheduling engine. A "what to trim" feature has to define, in code, some heuristic for "this card/deck isn't working" — that's an entirely new algorithm surface, adjacent to but distinct from SM-2, that now needs its own correctness bar. Nobody in this room has spec'd what "trim" means precisely, and if we ship it vague, we've just recreated the exact "plausibly right, not provably right" trap that DEC-prompt_contract-001 exists to prevent — except this time for a feature nobody asked for. Same problem with "exam mode presets" — presets implying different session-chunking or interruption behavior for a subset of users is a second code path through the one place (the review loop) that absolutely must stay singular and battle-tested. Every net-new surface Codex is proposing multiplies the number of things that can silently be wrong, in a project whose own priority order says SM-2 correctness beats everything, including monetization creativity. I'll die on this hill: any subscription design that adds new decision logic instead of gating existing, already-speced features is scope creep wearing a business-model costume, and it needs "explicit later-phase justification" per DEC-prompt_contract-006 that nobody has given it here.

So I'm picking my own model, but let me stress-test it instead of just repeating it, because Codex's underlying worry — "is a bare deck cap actually worth paying for" — deserves a real answer, not a wave-off. Here's the concrete numbers I want locked: free tier = up to 3 active (non-archived, non-demo) decks, unlimited cards per deck, full SM-2, full review flow, and — conceding a point to Codex here — the basic Stats screen shows the retention rate and today's due count for free, because a single number isn't a differentiator worth hiding and showing it costs us nothing while making the free app feel less like a trial. Paid unlocks: unlimited decks, the 30-day forecast chart and daily-history chart specifically (the two views that only get useful once you have real multi-week/multi-deck history — exactly the moment a serious user cares), CSV import, and the daily reminder. That's four concrete unlocks, all already-built features, zero new algorithms, and it still answers "why would I pay" honestly: because you have more than three subjects going, or you want to see your trend over time, or you want to bulk-import instead of hand-typing 200 cards, or you want a nudge so you don't break your streak. That's real utility, not a toggle on a cosmetic skin.

Now let me actually run the failure modes, because that's my job in this chair. Lapsed subscription: a user had 5 decks, cancels, now over the cap. My answer — those decks and their full review history are retained untouched in the store, they just get flagged locked and excluded from "all decks" review scope and from the deck-creation/edit affordance; a locked deck badge with "resubscribe to review this deck" is a designed state, not a silent disappearance. This needs a concrete test: subscribe, create 5 decks, review some cards, cancel/expire (or simulate via StoreKit config), relaunch, verify all 5 decks + full history still readable in a "manage decks" list even though only 3 are reviewable, and verify no card data or schedule data was deleted. Second failure mode: what happens to a card's due-state while its deck is locked? Time doesn't stop — a locked deck's cards keep aging past their due date the whole time you're not subscribed. If you resubscribe eight months later, do you get slammed with a backlog of "due" cards that accumulated while locked? Yes, and that's actually fine and correct — SM-2 has always tracked wall-clock elapsed time, not usage time, and pretending otherwise (freezing due-state while locked) would be the actual bug, a second, secret scheduling behavior contingent on entitlement, which is precisely what [REDACTED:high_entropy] forbids. So the spec has to say explicitly: locking a deck hides it from review and stats aggregation, it never freezes or alters its SM-2 state.

Third failure mode, and this is the one I think both of you are underweighting: demo decks and the cap. If demo data seeds two decks and the free cap is 3, a fresh install with demo data on effectively gives the user only 1 real deck of headroom before hitting the paywall, which reads as a bait-and-switn the moment they turn off demo mode expecting more room and it not being obvious why. Fix: demo decks explicitly do not count against the deck cap at all, in either direction — never counted, whether present or not — and that has to be enforced in the exact same counting function everywhere the cap is checked (deck-creation gate, Settings display of "2 of 3 decks used"), the same "one shared function, never reimplemented per screen" discipline we already locked in for due-date computation. That's the concrete detail I want written into this phase's output verbatim, because it's the kind of interaction bug that won't show up until QA actually toggles demo mode with a near-full deck list, and by then it's a live-app complaint, not a design review note.

Last thing — Codex, your "review integrity pack" language is doing a lot of work to make net-new features sound like they're still inside scope, but "deeper retention confidence stats" and "CSV validation diagnostics for big imports" are two different asks hiding in one phrase. If what you actually mean by the second one is just more detailed per-row error output in the CSV preview screen we're already building, I'm fine with that — that's polish on feature 5, not a new feature, and it's a good idea. But say that specifically, not "diagnostics pack," because the vague version is exactly what gets waved through review and then costs us a month of ambiguous scope later. I'm calling this: three-deck free cap, forecast+history charts and CSV import and reminders behind the subscription, retention-rate and due-count free, demo decks never counted, locked decks preserved-not-deleted with SM-2 state still advancing in real time. If Codex wants to keep any analytics idea, it has to be re-described as a concrete enhancement to an already-locked feature (e.g., "the existing retention chart also shows a per-deck breakdown," not "a new weekly recommendation engine"), or it doesn't make this brief.
